final_answer:
Short answer: probably not as a categorical matter, but it depends on facts the hypothetical leaves open. The claim could succeed only if the dispersal order and arrests lacked a lawful basis. Peaceful protest in a public forum is core First Amendment activity, and government may not disperse or arrest people merely because of the message, a generalized fear of disorder, or a hostile audience. Edwards v. South Carolina, 372 U.S. 229 (1963); Cox v. Louisiana, 379 U.S. 536 (1965); Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444 (1969) (advocacy is unprotected only if directed to and likely to produce imminent lawless action); Forsyth County v. Nationalist Movement, 505 U.S. 123 (1992) (no heckler's veto). But the First Amendment does not immunize a gathering from content-neutral time, place and manner regulation. Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 491 U.S. 781 (1989). Streets and traffic are legitimately regulated, and stepping into the roadway is not protected. Police may disperse an assembly that has become genuinely unlawful or presents a clear and present danger of imminent violence or serious obstruction, and may arrest those who knowingly refuse to comply with a lawful, adequately communicated order.

Application. (1) Dispersal order. The stated rationales were 'concern about traffic disruptions' and 'potential for escalation.' Generalized fear of escalation and a couple of verbal arguments with passers-by, with a mostly sidewalk-bound, peaceful crowd, is thin under Edwards and Cox, where peaceful demonstrators could not be punished because onlookers might react. Occasional street incursions could support a narrower, content-neutral response (clearing the roadway, targeted arrests for obstruction) rather than ending the whole assembly. The order is therefore vulnerable if police cannot articulate specific, imminent unlawful conduct (blocking traffic for a sustained period, violence, threats). (2) Illinois law. Illinois mob action, 720 ILCS 5/25-1, includes a Class A misdemeanor for a participant in a mob action who does not withdraw when commanded by a peace officer, but it requires an underlying mob action (force or violence disturbing the public peace, or assembly to commit an offense); peaceful protest does not meet it. Disorderly conduct, 720 ILCS 5/26-1(a)(1), requires an unreasonable act that alarms or disturbs another and provokes a breach of the peace. A Chicago municipal ordinance on disorderly conduct/failure to obey a police order may also be invoked, but I did not retrieve it; it must be checked. (3) Arrests and Fourth Amendment overlay. Whether arrests for failure to disperse violate the Constitution turns mainly on probable cause. In the Seventh Circuit, Vodak v. City of Chicago, 639 F.3d 738 (7th Cir. 2011), (as reported in secondary summaries I could access) held fact questions precluded summary judgment on probable cause for mass arrests at a 2003 anti-war protest, including whether the dispersal order was effectively communicated and whether the crowd was peaceable, and recognized that police cannot lawfully arrest people they have no good reason to believe knew they were violating an order where no threat to safety exists. Thayer v. Chiczewski, 705 F.3d 237 (7th Cir. 2012), concerned a Chicago dispersal and arrests of anti-war protesters; I could not retrieve it and do not state its holding. Probable cause for arrest, even if the dispersal was ill-advised, generally defeats a Fourth Amendment false-arrest claim, and qualified immunity is a significant obstacle for individual officers in the absence of clearly established law. Monell liability for the City requires a policy or custom.

Bottom line: On the stated facts (peaceful, mostly on sidewalk, no clear evidence of unlawful conduct, only generalized traffic and escalation concerns), the dispersal order and arrests are constitutionally vulnerable and a First Amendment challenge is plausible, but there is no per se violation. The outcome turns on (a) how much the crowd actually blocked traffic and for how long, (b) whether specific indicia of imminent violence existed, (c) whether the order was audible, clear, gave a reasonable opportunity and route to disperse, (d) whether the arrested persons were individually identified as unlawfully obstructing, and (e) the ordinance or statute charged. Where the order was lawful and properly communicated, the arrests for non-compliance are likely supported by probable cause and defensible; if the assembly was peaceful and the order unjustified, arrests may be unconstitutional, though officers may still have qualified immunity. Caveat: several primary sources (Edwards, Cox, Brandenburg, Forsyth County, Ward, Thayer, Vodak full text, statutes' full text) could not be fetched because of network blocks; these are cited from background knowledge or secondary search summaries and flagged unverified. Also not examined: any 2025 consent decrees or injunctions involving Chicago protest policing, and the separate federal-agent protest litigation in the Northern District of Illinois, which concerns federal not CPD conduct.

Standard for dispersing an assembly: imminent lawless action, clear and present danger, hostile audience/heckler's veto
Content-neutral time/place/manner regulation of street/traffic obstruction
Illinois and Chicago substantive offenses underlying failure to disperse (mob action, disorderly conduct, municipal ordinance)

claims.text: Peaceful protest in a public forum is protected, and generalized fear of disorder or hostile reaction does not justify dispersal or arrest.
Government may regulate street obstruction and disperse assemblies posing imminent unlawful conduct, so no per se violation; outcome is fact-dependent.
Failure-to-disperse arrests are lawful if the order was lawful, clearly communicated and probable cause existed; Seventh Circuit treats communication and peaceable character as fact questions.
Illinois mob action and disorderly conduct statutes require more than peaceful assembly.
